bottom_line: In 2289 patients with severe chronic heart failure, carvedilol vs placebo reduced the combined risk of death or hospitalization for a cardiovascular reason by 27% (95% CI, 16% to 37%).
implications: These data support that, in the studied euvolemic severe chronic heart failure population, carvedilol (vs placebo) lowered time-to-event risks for death or cardiovascular hospitalization by 27% (95% CI, 16% to 37%) and for death or heart-failure hospitalization by 31% (95% CI, 19% to 41%), with lower annual mortality (19.7% to 12.8%) and fewer serious adverse events (45.5% to 39.0%). The findings do not establish effects in patients excluded from enrollment (e.g., those requiring intensive care or receiving intravenous vasodilators or positive inotropic agents), because such patients were not enrolled.

major_points.text: Randomized, double-blind trial in severe chronic heart failure with EF <25%, comparing carvedilol vs placebo over an average of 10.4 months.
major_points.quote: We randomly assigned 2289 patients with symptoms of heart failure at rest or on minimal exertion and with an ejection fraction ⬍25% (but not volume-overloaded) to double-blind treatment with either placebo (n⫽1133) or carvedilol (n⫽1156) for an average of 10.4 months.

major_points.text: Carvedilol reduced death or cardiovascular hospitalization (Kaplan-Meier 1-year cumulative risks 41.6% vs 30.2%) with a 27% lower risk (95% CI 16% to 37%).
major_points.quote: Kaplan-Meier 1-year cumulative risks of 41.6% and 30.2%, respectively. These differences reflected a 27% lower risk as a result of treatment with carvedilol (95% CI, 16% to 37%), P⫽0.00002

major_points.text: Carvedilol reduced death or heart-failure hospitalization (Kaplan-Meier 1-year cumulative risks 37.9% vs 25.5%) with a 31% lower risk (95% CI 19% to 41%).
major_points.quote: Kaplan-Meier 1-year cumulative risks of 37.9% and 25.5%, respectively. These differences reflected a 31% lower risk in the carvedilol group (95% CI, 19% to 41%), P⫽0.000004
